title: StreamAhead: Real-Time Streaming Video Question Answering via Adaptive Precomputation
abstract: Real-time streaming video question answering with vision-language models must answer queries that arrive at any time with low latency while sustaining the video-processing rate required by the application. Existing systems construct key-value (KV) caches for the entire video as it arrives, although a query typically uses only a few of the preceding frames as evidence. This highlights a fundamental trade-off: performing more computation as video arrives reduces query-time computation but can increase processing lag, whereas deferring computation can increase the video-processing rate but requires additional query-time computation for retrieved content. We present StreamAhead, an algorithm-system co-design that exploits this trade-off through adaptive precomputation: dynamically controlling how much computation to complete for each video segment before a query arrives. StreamAhead encodes video segments independently and lets each remain at a different representation level, from inexpensive visual features to costly KV caches, completing KV caches only for the retrieved segments when a query arrives. StreamAhead profiles offline the cost of advancing a segment to each representation level. Its runtime uses these profiles to schedule segment computation concurrently with query execution, pipelining it across heterogeneous CPU and GPU resources while maintaining the required video-processing rate. StreamAhead achieves accuracy competitive with state-of-the-art methods with up to 10.4x lower time-to-first-token (TTFT), and up to 5.9x lower TTFT than state-of-the-art streaming systems. It sustains 30 FPS with P95 TTFT under 0.5 s, and up to 57 FPS with P95 TTFT under 2 s. To our knowledge, StreamAhead is the first real-time streaming video QA system with competitive accuracy, setting a new Pareto frontier between video-processing rate and TTFT.

title: A Distribution-Free Separation Between Learned and Fixed Features
abstract: The success of neural networks is largely attributed to their ability to learn useful representations from training data. However, known results that prove a computational advantage of learned features over fixed ones are restricted to specific input distributions. We settle the COLT open question of Feldman, Kamath, and Srebro (2026) by showing that this advantage can persist in the distribution-free setting. We construct a family of hypothesis classes that can be efficiently learned by a natural gradient-based algorithm on a two-layer ReLU network, but cannot be represented by linear predictors over any fixed feature map with polynomial dimension (and runtime). Specifically, for any sufficiently small error and any sufficiently large runtime budget R (depending on the error), there exists a hypothesis class that the neural network learns under any input distribution to the desired expected classification error in time at most R, while the dimension complexity (governing the dimension needed by linear predictors) is superpolynomial in R.

title: Pre-Query Retention with Bounded Bit and Word Retrieval
abstract: An agent can retain information before receiving a future question and later retrieve evidence from an archive. Evaluating this arrangement requires accounting for both retained information and the width of each retrieval response. Decision-tree capacity bounds describe individual sets of distinguishable records, but a memory writer must encode every possible record before the query is known. We study fixed-length retention beside an immutable binary archive, with a worst-case limit on raw bit or word reads. We characterize feasible one-bit-read memory cells and construct encoders that partition the complete record space. Supporting pairwise exclusive disjunction and conjunction with one bit read is equivalent to supporting every Boolean query. For multiple reads, we combine explicit encoders with decision-tree counting and an entropy converse. The word-read bounds differ by at most two retained bits when the read budget is at most half the archive length. Under an explicit condition on word width and archive length, raw-word caching attains the exact optimum among all writers. A related condition preserves this optimum under positive average error. Exhaustive checks validate the implementations. In a matched dialogue-agent study, a categorical sufficient statistic preserves source decisions with less storage and lower decoding latency than the universal encoder. A catalogue-specific index reduces private state further and requires additional shared storage. The results characterize how response width and future query structure determine retention requirements.

title: ZAC-Specialization: Collective Capability Provisioning Through Hardware–Role Co-Design in Heterogeneous Intelligent Agent Populations
abstract: Heterogeneous intelligent-agent populations are often designed by assigning different tasks to agents with different capabilities. However, task specialization alone does not determine whether every agent must independently possess the hardware and computational resources required to perform its assigned functions. A population may contain specialized agents whose capabilities are available to others through shared services, while individual agents retain only the hardware necessary for their own responsibilities. This paper proposes ZAC-Specialization, a research framework for jointly determining agent specialization, local hardware configuration, collective capability provisioning, and reliability-aware service allocation. The central design question is not simply which agent should execute a task, but which capabilities must be provisioned locally, which should be maintained by specialized providers, and how these decisions should change as workloads and operating conditions evolve. The proposed framework represents tasks through capability requirements, agents through configurable hardware and service profiles, and collective execution through capability-service assignments. A joint optimization formulation minimizes lifecycle hardware costs, execution costs, communication overhead, coordination costs, and expected failure losses, subject to task-feasibility, deadline, capacity, and reliability constraints. The paper introduces a distinction between local capability ownership and collective capability accessibility, a specialization–provisioning decision model, and an adaptive role-reconfiguration mechanism. It also develops analytical conditions for evaluating when specialization is economically beneficial, identifies limitations arising from correlated failures and provider bottlenecks, and proposes an experimental methodology comparing individual provisioning, fixed specialization, dynamic task allocation, and joint specialization–provisioning optimization. The framework is conceptual and does not claim demonstrated performance improvements. Its potential contribution must be established against existing research on heterogeneous multi-robot task allocation, capability-based coordination, and hardware–software co-design. The primary hypothesis is that jointly optimizing specialization and provisioning may reveal lower-cost feasible population configurations that cannot be identified by optimizing task allocation or individual hardware configurations in isolation.

title: Editing as Language: Teaching LLM Agents a Grammar for Native Context Editing
abstract: A synopsis in novels folds a story into a few lines; a function in code gathers many steps with a single execution. Context editing is native to language itself. In this paper, we propose the Native Context Editing (NCE) framework, which gives language model agents a grammar for natively editing their own context. By encoding context-editing operations in a grammar of dedicated special tokens, we teach the agents to invoke edits through the language itself. We train agents on iteratively constructed trajectory segments, with each teacher edit conditioned on the evolving context. This establishes context editing as an atomic and inherent capability of LLM agents, enabling them to dynamically modify their context as they generate responses over long-horizon reasoning and interaction. Compared with context-editing methods that learn to generate tool-use code within specific external harness environments, our approach integrates context editing as an internal mechanism of the model's native generation process, enabling better generalization across diverse real-world workflows. On four long-horizon agentic benchmarks (Terminal-Bench 2.0, SWE-bench Verified, SWE-bench Multilingual, and SWE-bench Pro), NCE improves the average task success rate over the base model by 5.6 percentage points for LongCat-Flash-Lite-Sparse and by 4.5 for Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, while reducing average token usage by 36% and 15%, respectively.

title: Does the authors' historical PPO configuration reproduce their released learning curves? Pre-registered replication of the Template-B output-reuse experiments at 16 minibatches (cycle 12R; third paper of a PhD on hybrid quantum–classical reinforcement learning)
abstract: AUTHORS Konstantinos Zervakis (Hellenic Army Academy); co-author Ilias Panagiotopoulos (Hellenic Army Academy). HOW THIS REGISTRATION DIFFERS FROM THE PREVIOUS ONE The cycle-12 registration (10.17605/OSF.IO/V7M6H) tests a mechanistic law on the published Template-B agent at the configuration of the authors' public scripts. This registration answers a point the authors raised in reply to our query of 2026-10-15: their published experiments were run with num_minibatches = 16, while the public scripts inherit num_minibatches = 4 from the released PPO class (num_steps 512, update_epochs 4 and learning rate 2.5e-4 are identical). The authors asked us to re-run an unentangled R = 4 run with the historical values. This step is pre-registered before any run; cycle 12 (running at registration time) is not changed by it. QUESTION At the historical configuration, are the released r4 and r16 curves (output-reuse factor R = 4 / 16; R replicas of the full circuit output vector feed the linear head) and the data-re-uploading L = 1 curve reproduced at nominal R, does the CNOT ring still fail, and are four-fold gradient steps operationally equivalent to four-fold output reuse? INSTRUMENTS AND ARMS (A) The authors' unmodified code (git commit 6b9897c, isolated environment hashed at the freeze), with the four historical values passed to their PPO class and asserted before training: none_R4_mb4 (the public configuration, never run before at nominal R = 4), none_R4_mb16, none_R16_mb16, ring_R4_mb16, ring_R16_mb16, dr_L1_none_R1_mb16; seeds 1200–1209; 100,000 steps (60 runs). (B) Our re-implementation of Template B (the one used in cycles 11 and 12), identical except for the minibatch count: none_R4_mb4, none_R4_mb16, none_R16_mb4, none_R16_mb16, ring_R4_mb4, ring_R4_mb16, ring_R16_mb16; seeds 1200–1229; 100,000 steps (210 runs). (F1) Fingerprint replays of the authors' code: the first three updates (1,536 steps of the 100,000-step schedule) for seeds 1–10, R in {4, 16}, num_minibatches in {4, 16}, with and without the authors' get_agent_info call (80 replays), compared with the clipfrac, approx_kl and value_loss series of the released r4/r16 event files. METRICS AND REGISTERED INPUTS Authors' metric: per seed, the mean return of training episodes ending at step ≥ 90,000 (identical computation for their CSV, our episode log and their TensorBoard files). Our metric J (instrument B only): 11 evaluation points × 32 episodes with sampled actions and common random numbers; AUC of J; "learns" = final J ≥ 0.20. The released per-seed values are registered in the frozen file with the SHA-256 of each event file: r4 (95.8, 98.6, 103.4, 72.5, 96.8, 163.3, 99.6, 113.4, 85.5, 137.7), r16 (389.0, 219.6, 146.3, 485.2, 407.0, 458.1, 415.2, 440.0, 354.1, 163.3), DR-L1 (43.0, 48.7, 41.6, 55.7, 51.9, 47.4, 42.0, 50.0, 46.6, 46.4). REGISTERED STATEMENTS (decision rules in the frozen file, section 6) P1: A none_R4_mb16 vs the released r4 — three outcomes: "not reproduced" (two-sided Welch p < 0.05 and exact label-permutation p < 0.05), "reproduced" (90 % CI of the difference of mean log returns within ± log 1.5, i.e. an equivalence test within a factor 1.5), otherwise "consistent". Expected: reproduced. P1-control: A none_R4_mb4 vs r4 — "differs" iff both p < 0.05 and the mean lies below the released mean. Expected: differs. P2: A none_R16_mb16 vs r16, same three outcomes (power allows at best "consistent"). Expected: consistent or reproduced. P3: the ring fails at 16 minibatches — at most 1 of 10 completed A seeds reaches an authors'-metric value ≥ 100 and at most 3 of 30 B seeds learn, in each mb16 ring arm. Expected: pass. P4: B paired contrast none_R4_mb16 − none_R16_mb4 on the AUC of J — EQ iff the 90 % CI lies within ± 0.03 ("four-fold steps interchangeable with four-fold reuse"). Expected: EQ. P5: B paired none_R16_mb16 − none_R4_mb16 > 0 (the output-reuse gain persists at 16 minibatches). Expected: positive beyond 0.05. P6: B paired none_R4_mb16 − none_R4_mb4 > 0 (the minibatch count matters). Expected: positive beyond 0.05. P7: A dr_L1_none_R1_mb16 vs the released DR-L1 curve, three outcomes. Expected: reproduced if PPO was held fixed across the authors' experiments. F1 (descriptive): a configuration is "identified" for a log set iff its replay matches all three series of updates 1–3 within 1e-5 (relative) for ≥ 8 of 10 seeds and no other configuration does; otherwise "not identified" (the closest configuration is reported, no claim). Expected: R = 4 (r4) and R = 16 (r16), both at 16 minibatches. Holm correction over {P4, P5, P6} only; P1, P1-control, P2 and P7 are decided by their own rules; P3 is a count rule. Completeness: ≥ 8/10 completed seeds (A) and ≥ 23/30 (B) per row; a crashed run is re-run once and then counted as missing. The wording each outcome licenses in the paper (for example "documentation gap in the public scripts" vs "unexplained" vs "the instruments disagree") is fixed in the frozen file. GATES (binding, logged before any main run) Every A run asserts num_steps 512, num_minibatches 16 (or 4 for the control), minibatch size 32 (128), update_epochs 4, learning rate 2.5e-4, annealing on, 100,000 total steps, and after training 12,544 (3,136) optimiser steps and 196 learning-rate entries ending at 1.276e-6, as in all 40 released files; the A smoke runs twice and the two logs must be identical except wall time. Instrument B reproduces a stored cycle-11 run bit for bit at 4 minibatches before anything else runs. The authors' environment is hashed and compared before F1, before the A smoke and before the A main runs. ORDER AND STATUS Freeze → this registration → cycle 12 finished → F1 → B → A → analysis by the unchanged pre-written statistics script. No run of this step exists at registration time. Everything through cycle 11, the authors' reply and the cycle-12 freeze are known; the cycle-12 results are not known at the freeze; no statement here uses a cycle-12 quantity. Later answers from the authors change no rule. FILES IN THIS REGISTRATION cycle12R_phase1_prereg.md (frozen text; SHA-256 953ae2c5579e7f8cbc32c73352fc65b4a77dcbf83154b2a0d42442a334608065), c12r_train.py (instrument-B runner), run_authors_mb16.py (instrument-A runner for the authors' code), c12r_f1.py (fingerprint replays), c12r_shipped.py (extraction of the released per-seed values), stats_c12r.py (pre-registered statistics; rules and wording as data), pipeline_c12r.sh (launcher), shipped_c12r.json (released per-seed values with event-file SHA-256), cycle12R_code_identity.txt (code commit 2eb68d4, runner, pre-registration and environment hashes), PROVENANCE_SHA256.txt, SHA256SUMS.txt, this README.

title: EmotiQ: A Quantum Residual Specialist Framework for Text Emotion Classification
abstract: Emotion classification from text is challenging because many affective states are distinguished by subtle linguistic signals and semantically overlapping boundaries. We investigate whether compact quantum modules can serve as targeted residual specialists that assist traditional classifiers on difficult emotion decisions. We introduce EmotiQ, a residual specialist framework for text emotion classification using a frozen transformer classifier as the primary decision maker, identifies challenging emotion boundaries from validation behavior, and trains boundary specialists, including quantum encodings, data re-uploading specialists, prototype and fidelity specialists, and kernel-based specialists. Specialists are permitted to intervene only when they satisfy validation-based admission criteria. We evaluate the framework across six text emotion classification datasets and establish traditional model baselines. Experimental results show that the admitted EmotiQ policy improves mean macro-F1 metrics over the baseline, and achieves positive gains on five of six datasets. Among the quantum components, ZZ interaction feature maps are the most consistently effective, yielding a mean macro-F1 improvement of +0.0030 and positive gains on four datasets. These findings suggest that current quantum NLP methods can be deployed as residual specialists that provide localized improvements under strong classical supervision.

title: CoRe-WM: Conditioned Response-State World Modeling for Longitudinal Treatment-Response Prediction in Breast DCE-MRI
abstract: Pathologic complete response (pCR) after neoadjuvant chemotherapy is a key prognostic indicator in aggressive breast cancer, yet existing prediction approaches either rely on pretreatment imaging alone, missing the patient's evolving response, or optimize multi-visit classifiers under direct outcome supervision, coupling representation learning with the clinical endpoint. We formulate longitudinal pCR prediction as a world-modeling problem and propose Conditioned Response-state World Modeling (CoRe-WM), which learns a latent state-transition model that predicts the next imaging state from the observed sequence. The transition function is conditioned on patient clinical profile and assigned therapy through additive shift and feature-wise modulation, enabling patient- and treatment-specific dynamics. A Factorized Response State pathway further decouples treatment-response dynamics from imaging appearance by encoding the structural prior that response manifests primarily in lesion morphology. After pretraining, all parameters are frozen and a linear readout predicts pCR at each clinical decision point. We evaluate CoRe-WM on I-SPY2 under five-fold cross-validation and assess cross-cohort transfer on I-SPY1. CoRe-WM achieves the highest discrimination among all evaluated methods at every prospective decision point, and demonstrates robust cross-cohort transfer. Ablation studies identify patient-profile conditioning and the factorized response pathway as the principal contributors. These results establish world-model-based representation learning as a promising framework for outcome prediction in oncology and beyond.

title: ChunavIQ: An Open, End-to-End Verifiable Remote-Voting Prototype for India's Legal and Identity Constraints, with Deniable Revoting, Hardware-Held Trustee Keys and Adversarial Dress Rehearsals
abstract: India runs the world's largest elections: about 970 million electors in 543 parliamentary constituencies in 2024. Any remote-voting proposal for India must fit its election law, its identity infrastructure and its scale, and must say what it does not solve. We present ChunavIQ, an open-source research prototype that combines established techniques (threshold ElGamal, zero-knowledge ballot proofs, deniable revoting, Terelius-Wikström verifiable shuffles, designated-verifier proofs and an append-only Merkle log) into a complete system adapted to Indian constraints. Voters register a phone with either Aadhaar or PAN; since PAN checks only a name and birth date, the PAN path adds a one-time code to the mobile number on the electoral roll and a face match. A voter may vote again at any time, and a vote at a polling station on polling day cancels the online ballot; nobody, including a coercer, can tell which ballot counted. One national key is shared among trustees whose shares stay inside hardware security modules. We contribute (i) the adapted protocol and two independent implementations with two independent verifiers that cross-check each other's records; (ii) a capacity model for 1-1.5 billion electors built from measured unit costs; (iii) an open dress-rehearsal method that runs a constituency election over HTTP under seven kinds of attack and publishes every request; and (iv) a provision-by-provision analysis of the Indian legal changes such a system would need. Every record we produced verified. A first rehearsal forced the largest constituency's full design rate onto one machine and recorded only 72-99% of honest ballots per phase; after fixes identified from its published metrics, a rehearsal at 78% of that rate recorded every honest ballot, 97-100% of them within 30 s, while refusing every attack. ChunavIQ uses synthetic data only and is not proposed for binding elections. Code: https://github.com/itsashiish/chunaviq (archived at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23442948). Demo: https://chunaviq.oglic.com

title: A Simulation-Driven Digital Workflow Integrating Bayesian Optimization for Early-Stage Process Design: A Methyl Acetate Production Case Study
abstract: Methyl acetate production via direct carbonylation of dimethyl ether and carbon monoxide involves strong nonlinear interactions among reactor operation, recycle structure, and energy consumption, making conventional simulation-based optimization computationally demanding. In this work, a data-driven framework integrating steady-state process simulation, surrogate modeling, and Bayesian optimization was developed for process intensification. A dataset of 2730 steady-state simulations was generated using a Python-based automated process simulation workflow and a structured design of experiments across the operating domain. Surrogate models were trained to predict carbon conversion yield (C-yield) and cost of specific energy consumption (C-SEC), with neural network-based models showing the best predictive performance and robustness. These models were integrated into a multi-objective Bayesian optimization framework to identify optimal operating regions. Results indicate that high C-yield (up to ~95%) can be achieved with reduced energy cost through lower recycle flow rates and compression demand. Pareto analysis revealed a nonlinear trade-off between C-yield and C-SEC, where further improvements near the conversion limit require disproportionately higher energy input. Validation against rigorous simulations showed deviations below 3% for C-yield and 10% for C-SEC.

title: Beyond the record: evaluating probabilistic AI weather forecasts deep in the tail
abstract: Can probabilistic artificial intelligence (AI) weather forecasts retain skill beyond their training domain? We compare four state-of-the-art AI models (ArchesWeatherGen, U-Cast, WeatherNext2 and GenCast-mini) with the physics-based IFS-ENS over land in 2022, at 1.5° resolution and lead times of 2--10 days. Monthly ERA5 records from 1979--2021 define common historical boundaries, and we characterize new records set in 2022 by their depth, i.e., the exceedance margin relative to local historical variability. Two proper scores, record-threshold weighted CRPS and Brier score, assess the magnitude and probability of record exceedances across all eligible cases, retaining both missed extremes and false alarms. Verified against ERA5, AI models outperform IFS-ENS for heat and cold records at almost every lead and depth. For heat, the advantage strengthens with depth, partly because IFS-ENS over-forecasts deep records, and largely persists for deeper records under HRES-fc0 verification. For wind, gains erode for deeper records and longer leads. Better tail scores can nevertheless coexist with aggregate probability deficits or surpluses, and some improvements arise chiefly on non-exceedances. Increasing underprediction on progressively more extreme observed subsets can also arise through outcome selection, even for an ideal conditional-mean forecast. These findings establish that native probabilistic AI ensembles retain, and for heat increase, their advantage over IFS-ENS as thresholds move beyond local records, although all advantages narrow with lead time. They caution against generalizing the extrapolation failure reported for deterministic AI forecasts to probabilistic systems, and motivate common verification conventions that separate comparative tail skill, performance on realized extremes, and probabilistic calibration.

title: Follow the Mixed Groups: Ridge-Tracking Gaussian Sampling for Zero-Variance Web Rollouts
abstract: Group relative policy optimization learns from a question only when the sampled responses disagree. A group that is entirely correct or entirely incorrect has zero reward variance and a zero advantage. On the Web, that group has already spent its searches and page fetches. Gaussian curricula aim the next batch at pass rates where a finite group can still mix. A Gaussian on the latest empirical rate treats every all-fail history as the same point, and a center stepped by the average signed change of those rates is pushed by prompts already stuck at 0 or 1. RIDGE keeps the Gaussian curriculum and changes the coordinate, the center, and the width. Each prompt carries a Beta posterior. The sampling weight is the marginal of a Gaussian target under a Gaussian approximation of that posterior, divided by a prediction of tool-call cost. The center and the width are an exponential smooth of the posterior means of groups that just came back mixed. All-correct and all-incorrect groups refresh the posterior and do not move the center. The GRPO update itself is unchanged. On two math backbones and a retrieval-augmented question answerer, RIDGE raises average accuracy by 3.4 and 2.9 points over GRPO and average exact match by 3.7 points, at 29.6\% fewer math rollouts and 32.7\% fewer tool calls than dynamic sampling.

title: Matched data, small gaps: a pre-registered comparison of fine-tuned classifiers, retrieval-prompted language models and a typed-decision model for intent and out-of-scope decisions
abstract: Before an assistant acts on a message, it decides whether the message is something it handles (scope) and what it asks for (intent). We ask which kind of system should make that decision given the same in-scope labelled data, and what moves a prompted model's scope decision. We compare a fine-tuned 150M classifier with retrieval-prompted 27–31B language models on three intent sets, in protocols frozen before any request; only the classifier also calibrates its scope decision on out-of-scope development items, and a hosted typed-decision model is a secondary system. On Banking77 the two are not significantly different, though equivalence within 2.5 points is not shown, and MASSIVE shows no stable ordering across four draws of held-out domains. The one significant pre-registered gap (CLINC150, 1.9 points for the language model) halves and is not significant on items we had never inspected (post hoc). The clearest finding concerns the second question. On fresh label-clean BANKING77-OOS items, retrieving in-scope examples lowered five models' rejection of same-domain out-of-scope requests by 19 to 30 points, while random examples moved it by 1 to 11. This is mainly a shift of the operating point towards acceptance, not a demonstrated loss of discrimination: at equal in-scope acceptance, the typed-decision model's rejection rose. Labelled out-of-scope examples raise rejection, mainly for the requests that retrieve them. We also report a label leak we found in BANKING77-OOS and the exploratory conclusions we withdrew.

title: Sequential Transfer Learning for Plant Disease Recognition Across Perennial Crop Domains Using MobileNetV2-CBAM
abstract: Purpose: This study investigates whether a learned disease-recognition representation can be progressively reused across distinct perennial crop domains and how its predictive behaviour changes as target-domain heterogeneity increases. Design/methodology/approach: A lightweight MobileNetV2 framework enhanced with the Convolutional Block Attention Module (CBAM) was evaluated through sequential transfer from Walnut to Cashew, Coffee and Mango, followed by validation on the heterogeneous ABCGMP six-crop benchmark. Each stage used the preceding model representation and was evaluated on an independent test set using complementary classification measures. Findings: Test accuracy increased from 75.76% for the Walnut baseline to 84.85% after CBAM integration, followed by 90.67% on Cashew, 100.00% on Coffee and 99.50% on Mango. The final ABCGMP evaluation achieved 88.44% accuracy, 81.49% Balanced Accuracy and 0.9949 ROC-AUC. The results show that substantial predictive capability was retained through successive crop transfers, while broader multi-crop heterogeneity introduced a measurable performance constraint. Originality: The study provides an empirical characterisation of sequential knowledge reuse across multiple perennial crop domains using a common lightweight attention-enhanced representation, extending evaluation beyond isolated source-to-target transfer.

title: Reinforcement learning on the EPRI AI-ccelerating Unit Commitment benchmark: diagnosing over-commitment and guiding MILP with learned policies
abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) is increasingly proposed as a fast solver for unit commitment (UC), but standalone agents remain far more expensive than mixed-integer linear programming (MILP). In the first study of RL on the 51-generator, 72-hour benchmark of the Electric Power Research Institute (EPRI) AI-ccelerating Unit Commitment competition, we trace this gap to the agents' own exploration, close most of it, and show that the resulting policy can accelerate an exact solver. In every configuration tested, Proximal Policy Optimisation (PPO) and an action-branching Deep Q-Network (DQN) trained from scratch committed about twice the units of a thermal-only MILP optimum, at 39-64% higher cost, whereas a merit-order rule came within 1.6-7% (10-24% when unserved energy is priced). When each unit's decision is sampled independently, spare units insure against random de-commitments. Consistent with this, injecting exploration noise during fine-tuning enlarged a lean policy's fleet, a reward without shaping terms did not remove the over-commitment, and under their training noise the agents outperformed the rule subjected to comparable noise. Imitating the MILP solutions and fine-tuning conservatively brought PPO within 2.6% of the optimum, and these policies had the lowest penalised cost of any evaluated (about 5%). Fixing the fine-tuned policy's confident decisions made the MILP 3.8-8.5 times faster within 0.10-0.25% of the best solution, with a smaller worst case than an imitation-only policy fixing as many variables (1.1% against 8.9%). Because dispatch method and benchmark scope alone shift the reported optimality ratio by up to 3.6% and 9%, we propose a reporting protocol.

title: Conformal Prediction-Enabled Sequence-level Policy Optimization for Reasoning Language Models
abstract: Reinforcement learning improves the reasoning capability of large language models through verifiable rewards for mathematical and coding tasks. In token-level methods such as GRPO, clipping acts on individual token ratios while the reward and advantage apply to a complete response. Recent sequence-level methods align these units but still use fixed clipping bands, whose tail probabilities change as the score distribution evolves. We propose Conformal Prediction-Enabled Sequence-level Policy Optimization (CSPO), which adaptively calibrates sequence-level clipping bounds using recent training statistics. The resulting band targets a specified marginal tail budget and adapts to policy drift; calibration conditional on response length requires additional assumptions. We bound the probability that a fresh score falls outside the band by the target miscoverage level plus explicit CDF discrepancy and drift terms. Under additional moment conditions, this bound also controls the objective and gradient error relative to the unclipped GSPO power surrogate. Experiments with the Qwen3-1.7B series show improvements over GSPO on difficult mathematical reasoning benchmarks and ALFWorld, with clipping endpoints that adapt during training.

title: VoiceGuard: An Evaluation-Honest, Multi-Signal Decision Layer for Real-Time Voice-Clone Detection in High-Stakes Telephone Calls
abstract: VoiceGuard: An Evaluation-Honest, Multi-Signal Decision Layer for Real-Time Voice-Clone Detection in High-Stakes Telephone Calls This paper investigates the generalization limitations of speech anti-spoofing systems for detecting voice-clone fraud in telephone calls. It examines evaluation artifacts in the ASVspoof 2019 Logical Access benchmark and re-evaluates the published AASIST model using an anti-shortcut evaluation protocol. The paper proposes VoiceGuard, a multi-signal decision layer that combines acoustic spoof detection, speaker consistency, prosodic features, and call context to generate ALLOW, VERIFY, or ESCALATE recommendations. It also introduces a feature-only audit log to support transparency and human review. Additionally, a five-language pilot study evaluates the transferability of an English-trained detector across Indian languages, highlighting the challenges of multilingual voice-clone detection. The work emphasizes evaluation integrity, cross-dataset generalization, explainable decision-making, and the need for further validation before deployment in high-stakes environments. Authors: Ghanshyam Kumavat, Sunil Saini, and Vicky PukaleAffiliation: Department of Computer Engineering, Vidyalankar Institute of Technology, Mumbai, India.

title: Auditing Tool Traces in Agentic LLMs: Source Localization and Counterfactual Dependence Testing
abstract: Agentic LLMs increasingly support scientific prediction by grounding decisions in external evidence. In biology, they promise accurate, interpretable predictions for important problems by integrating complex experimental and computational evidence. However, serialized tool results can contain hidden label shortcuts, such as dataset identifiers or template artifacts, that create apparent success without biological reasoning. To address this risk, we introduce a two-stage audit. Stage 1, Per-Tool TF-IDF Decomposition (PT2D), localizes label-predictive patterns to individual tool results while avoiding signal dilution in the concatenated tool trace. Stage 2, Token-Class Redaction, counterfactually tests whether the frozen LLM depends on the localized shortcut. We apply this audit to TCR-pMHC binding, where tool augmentation substantially outperforms a no-evidence baseline. At face value, this suggests that the LLM has learned to use scientific evidence. The audit overturns this interpretation: PT2D localizes the strongest signal to identifiers in one tool result, and redacting them reduces performance to chance. These findings show how hidden label shortcuts can masquerade as scientific reasoning or discovery, motivating source-level audits before benchmark gains are trusted.

title: MPIG: Multi-angle Polarization Image Generation from a Single Polarization Observation
abstract: Polarization imaging provides informative cues for material analysis, scene understanding, and visual perception. However, acquiring complete polarization observations typically requires specialized hardware and multi-angle measurements, thereby increasing system complexity and limiting practical deployment. In this work, we address the problem of predicting the missing $45^\circ$, $90^\circ$, and $135^\circ$ polarization views from a single $0^\circ$ observation by leveraging a learned scene prior. To this end, we propose MPIG (Multi-angle Polarization Image Generation), a Swin Transformer-based framework that couples cross-angle feature interaction with residual decoding to predict angle-dependent intensity variations while preserving shared scene structure. Specifically, measured Stokes differences and polarization-strength-aware supervision guide the recovery of polarization modulation, orientation, and magnitude, while low-rank factorization further reduces the decoding cost. We also construct HighPol, a large-scale real-world polarization dataset comprising 5,474 groups of high-resolution four-angle polarization images collected from diverse indoor and outdoor scenes. Experimental results demonstrate improved image and polarization accuracy, achieving 29.729 dB PSNR, 0.9505 SSIM, and $21.514^\circ$ AoLP MAngE while requiring 85.86 M parameters and 1.126 T FLOPs. Furthermore, downstream validation on glass and semantic-segmentation tasks suggests that the generated polarization images can preserve task-relevant information, demonstrating the effectiveness of MPIG and the practical utility of predicted polarization observations for downstream vision applications.

title: Neural Networks with Differentiable Belief-Function Layers
abstract: Yager's 1987 rule of combination $\boxplus$ was proposed on epistemic grounds: under high conflict, mass should be redistributed to ignorance rather than renormalised onto the class simplex. We observe that backpropagation needs the same rule: Dempster's normaliser $(1{-}κ)^{-1}$, where $κ$ is the conflict mass, puts a $(1{-}κ)^{-2}$ term in the gradient that diverges exactly when evidence sources disagree, while Yager's $\boxplus$ is bilinear and has no such term. Building on this, we construct a deep evidential pipeline in which every mass in the chain from heads to output is a valid Dempster--Shafer mass function, combined by Yager's rule. The output mass on the ignorance set, $m(Θ)$, serves as the network's ``I do not know'' signal. The network is fit to hard labels and never sees an annotator distribution, yet $m(Θ)$ orders human disagreement in two modalities, visual and linguistic. Dempster's rises too and ranks contested inputs about as well, but its normaliser divides the conflict out: Yager's vacuity is $9\times$ larger on the most contested CIFAR-10H images, so only Yager's is readable as an amount of ignorance without recalibration. For out-of-distribution detection it is competitive with strong single-pass baselines, while the clamped Dempster variant that scores higher becomes gradient-unstable once the clamp is removed.

title: Where Groups Split: A Probe Prior for Nonzero Within-Group Variance in RL Post-Training
abstract: Group relative policy optimization learns from a prompt only when the rewards in the sampled group disagree. With a binary verifier, a group that is entirely correct or entirely incorrect has within-group variance zero and a zero advantage. Uniform sampling continues to spend rollouts on prompts that are unanimous now and stay unanimous as training goes on. Pass rate is a weak forecast of that future. Two prompts at the same pass rate can move apart: one into the range where a finite group splits, and one toward a ceiling where the group becomes unanimous again. Aperture estimates the later pass rate from a short probe. A small subset of the pool is trained with the same recipe, every prompt is scored on the base model and on the probe model, and the two pass rates are plugged into the probability that a group of the training size is all wrong or split. The resulting weight is a static prior. It can be used alone or multiplied by an online scheduler, and the GRPO update is left as it is. On mathematical and logical reasoning with 1.7B and 4B models, the prior improves greedy accuracy over uniform GRPO and raises the fraction of groups with a nonzero advantage. The same prior still helps when it is combined with dynamic sampling or with selective rollouts.

title: DAGLoop: Aligning Method Design with Experimental Feedback in Automated AI Research
abstract: Automated AI research agents aim to improve machine learning methods by iteratively proposing, implementing, and evaluating candidate methods. Existing work uses the outcome of each evaluation to determine how the next candidate should be revised for performance improvement. However, a candidate often combines multiple design decisions, and its overall outcome alone does not reveal which decisions produced their expected effects, whether their required conditions were satisfied, or which decisions should be retained or revised. Inspired by ablation studies in the machine learning community, we propose DAGLoop to test the expected effect of a design decision by comparing implementations with and without that decision while preserving the other decisions it requires. Specifically, DAGLoop translates each design decision's rationale into a testable expectation and pairs it with a targeted experiment, forming an experimental specification for assessing the expected effect under its required conditions. Using these specifications, we formulate ablation planning as the construction of a directed acyclic graph (DAG) from the candidate method's design: nodes associate decisions with tests, and edges encode dependencies. The DAG specifies which decisions each experiment must retain and supports joint tests when an expected effect requires several decisions to act together. Outcomes are recorded with the tested decisions, expectations, and conditions to form structured research memory. This memory guides the agent in retaining experimentally supported decisions, revising unsupported ones, and planning further experiments when the evidence is unresolved. Experiments on dozens of research tasks demonstrate substantial performance improvements achieved by DAGLoop across diverse executable research settings. Code and evaluation scripts are available at https://github.com/deng34567/DAGLoop.

title: Residential Construction Image Dataset Using CSI Divisions for Deep Learning-based Object Detection
abstract: Accurate recognition of construction site elements is essential for the application of deep learning (DL) in the construction industry. Despite rapid advances in computer vision, the adoption of DL in construction has been limited by the lack of structured, publicly available datasets aligned with established industry standards. To address this gap, we introduce the Residential Construction Dataset Using CSI Divisions (ResCD-CSI) image dataset, a manually labeled image benchmark organized according to the divisional structure defined by the Construction Specifications Institute (CSI). The dataset comprises high-resolution images collected from active residential construction sites across the United States, capturing diverse building components, materials, and equipment under real-world conditions. In total, 16,365 objects spanning 14 major CSI divisions were precisely annotated using bounding boxes, ensuring consistency and reliability for object detection tasks. By aligning with the CSI divisional framework, ResCD-CSI establishes a standardized resource that bridges construction practice with computer vision research and supports the development of Artificial Intelligence-driven solutions for residential construction monitoring.

title: Where and Why Search-Augmented LLMs Fail When Reasoning over Rapidly Evolving Knowledge
abstract: As the world changes, new information is published while older records remain online. This complicates reasoning for large language models (LLMs), which must retrieve evidence and resolve conflicts to determine which information remains valid. Existing evaluations treat information seeking as a black box, revealing little about where and why LLMs fail. To address this gap, we introduce TREK, a suite of three components: TREKTRACE is a plug-and-play framework that attributes failures to specific stages of retrieval and reasoning. We apply it to TREKBENCH-WILD, a meta-benchmark of real-world questions that require complex reasoning over rapidly evolving knowledge. Surprisingly, the main bottleneck is post-retrieval reasoning rather than retrieval: frontier models are often misled by conflicting evidence even after retrieving all the information needed to answer. To study this bottleneck, we build TREKBENCH-CTRL, a controlled benchmark with distractors spanning temporality, relevance, and trustworthiness, and show that benchmarks dominated by outdated distractors substantially underestimate task difficulty. Together, TREK provides a testbed for diagnosing and improving reasoning over rapidly evolving knowledge.

title: Beyond Factual Accuracy: A Benchmark for Evaluating Perspective Alignment in LLMs
abstract: Large Language Models often generate factually correct responses that fail to maintain user-requested perspectives, blending multiple perspectives and forcing users to filter through unwanted information---a perspective control failure that factual accuracy metrics cannot detect. We introduce PerspectiveBench, a benchmark quantifying perspective alignment by constructing scenarios where multiple valid reasoning paths coexist, and propose the Perspective Alignment Score (PAS) to measure adherence to specified perspectives. Experiments reveal that state-of-the-art models successfully include target content but fail to exclude non-requested perspectives. Providing documents through RAG improves factual grounding but does not resolve perspective drift, as models prioritize comprehensive coverage over strict user constraints. Code and data are available at https://github.com/sunghoon014/PerspectiveBench.

title: Before the Point of No Return: Identifying Irreversible Decision Windows in Memory-Augmented Agents
abstract: Memory-augmented agents reuse past experience across long-horizon tasks, but a task-wrong (conflicting) memory is adopted early and its damage is often irreversible in the environment. We reproduce the MemTrapBench compliance-trap protocol and measure, step by step, where a conflicting memory first changes behavior, how far that change carries, and whether the agent can undo it, localizing a threshold X past which the trajectory is irreversibly bound for failure. We then test decision-window interventions: mechanical deliberation is inert on both a 9B and a 1.6T-parameter model, while a semantic intervention that demotes memory from authority to candidate is two-sided, helping on heterogeneous (mixed) memory and hurting on uniformly wrong memory, which bounds what a decision-layer intervention can and cannot do.

title: Argument Reasoning
abstract: Abstract Reasoning is the heart of argumentation—so much that some researchers might equate the terms reasoning and argumentation . This is because, conceptually, an argument manifests a reasoning process (or process step) in natural language: the relation that it defines from one or more premises to a conclusion instantiates the act of giving a reason, or reasons, to support a claim. In a broader sense, though, argumentation comprises more than just reasoning. As the previous chapters on perspective and quality assessment have emphasized, subjective viewpoints and perceptions are inherent to argumentation, and rhetoric and dialectic are important in any real-world argumentation setting. Thus, reasoning can be understood as the part of argumentation that describes how people infer new (or hidden) information from given information through the use or exchange of arguments. As such, reasoning is where the NLP tasks of analysis and synthesis meet. In this chapter, we discuss some main strands of NLP research that model key aspects of reasoning, given previously mined or otherwise structured arguments.

title: Modaliff: A Unified Token Diffusion Model for Any-to-Any Generation
abstract: Any-to-any generation seeks a single model that translates flexibly among text, image, and audio, yet existing approaches either require fully aligned multimodal tuples or a shared representation that suppresses modality-specific structure. We introduce Modaliff, a novel token-based diffusion model that learns from widely available bimodal pairs while preserving each modality in its native latent sequence. Modaliff assembles conditions and targets into a unified token sequence, with per-token attributes to disambiguate token identities and role-based positional embedding to preserve each modality's internal structure across sequence layouts. This design enables a single denoiser to support diverse generation tasks without task-specific architectural changes or a shared cross-modal latent space. Beyond one-to-one generation, Modaliff supports multiple conditions either by combining single-condition predictions at inference or by lightweight finetuning on captions that jointly describe multiple inputs. Experiments across text, image, and audio show that Modaliff achieves the best fidelity among any-to-any models on most generation tasks while using substantially fewer parameters and training data.

title: AdaFedXplain: Adaptive Federated Learning with Explainable AI for Ransomware Detection
abstract: Attacks using ransomware have developed into complex multiphase campaigns that target vital infrastructure, resulting in annual damages of billions of dollars. Conventional detection techniques are ineffective against zero-day variations, and privacy issues are raised by centralized machine learning algorithms. Federated learning allows for cooperative model training without data sharing, however current FL approaches suffer from explainability issues, high communication cost, and non-IID data heterogeneity. In this study, we present AdaFedXplain, an explainable AI-based adaptive federated learning system for ransomware detection. Our approach includes progressive XGBoost complexity to avoid overfitting, a decaying learning rate schedule for stable convergence, and dynamic client grading based on ransomware prevalence and data sufficiency. Using 62,485 real-world ransomware samples from four OS-based non-IID clients, we compare AdaFedXplain against FedAvg, FedProx, and SCAFFOLD. According to experimental data, AdaFedXplain outperforms all baselines with 99.59% detection accuracy and 99.64% F1-score while cutting energy usage by 75%, latency by 65%, and communication overhead by 75%. The ablation investigation demonstrates that every element enhances performance. Security analysts can use SHAP explainability to identify important PE header characteristics that influence detection decisions. Our system provides a collaborative ransomware detection solution that is efficient and interpretable, while reducing privacy risks through federated learnings data-local training paradigm.

title: Dual-Slot: From Serial Loops to Parallel Slots in Language Models
abstract: Looped language models increase computational depth by repeatedly applying shared layers, offering a way to improve model quality without adding parameters. However, sequential dependencies between loop iterations increase autoregressive decoding latency. We introduce Dual-Slot, an architecture that reorganizes serial looped computation into parallel latent and prediction slots. Rather than waiting for the current token's latent computation to finish, the prediction slot combines the previous token's deep latent state with the current representation, while the latent slot produces a state for the next decoding step. This shifts the latent dependency across adjacent tokens, replacing two sequential module invocations with a single paired invocation while preserving standard autoregressive generation. To preserve token-level parallelism during training, we use a small number of Jacobi iterations to refine latent states across the sequence in parallel. Experiments on Qwen-style dense and mixture-of-experts (MoE) models show consistent improvements in language modeling and average downstream accuracy. On the 1B dense model, Dual-Slot reduces Pile validation perplexity from 7.25 to 7.00 and improves average five-shot accuracy across nine task configurations by 2.26 percentage points. After supervised fine-tuning, it improves zero-shot GSM8K accuracy by 5.83 and 3.49 percentage points for the 1B dense and A0.6B MoE models, respectively. Across the evaluated batch sizes, Dual-Slot retains 93.1-96.5% of vanilla decoding throughput for the dense model and 98.1-99.6% for the MoE model.

title: How Far Can the Gemma 4 Speech Encoder Go Without Changing Its Weights? Saudi and Gulf Arabic Speech Recognition with a Frozen and an Adapter-Augmented Encoder
abstract: We study the 305M-parameter audio encoder shared by Gemma 4 and EmbeddingGemma 2 (bit-identical to that of Gemma 4 E2B except for the final audio-embedding projection) for Saudi and Gulf Arabic speech recognition, without changing any of its pretrained weights; the adapters of our adapted system are additive and kept separate. A frozen system trains only a 22.6M-parameter CTC reader over a learned mix of four intermediate encoder layers and the encoder output; an adapted system adds 3.1M low-rank adapter parameters, a 41.5M-parameter hybrid CTC/attention reader and joint decoding with a sub-word language model. Against Cohere Transcribe Arabic (2.07B parameters), re-run on identical audio, the frozen system trails in word error rate (WER) but is not significantly different in character error rate (CER) on five of six human-labelled conditions, while running 3.4 times faster on CPU with greedy decoding. The adapted system is not significantly different in WER on a public Saudi customer-service call (19.20% against 19.27%) and on clean Emirati speech, is significantly better on telephone-coded Emirati speech, has a significantly lower CER on all six conditions of these sets, and beats a 0.6B recogniser fine-tuned on SADA in WER on all six; it still trails Cohere in WER on long-form Saudi speech. On a blind, human-corrected public call-centre sample it ranks 4 of 15 systems, behind three commercial APIs (significantly only one) and ahead of the other self-hostable systems by point estimate. An optimised joint decoder runs it at 139 times real time on one GPU. We also find, on our data, that references made by correcting machine drafts favour the drafting system. Code and public-set results are released.

title: Atoms, Not Knowledge: What Production-Scale Addressed-Memory Writes Deposit
abstract: Deterministic hash-addressed conditional memory permits local post-hoc knowledge injection. Extending arXiv:2610.21553's bounded-feasibility audit rejecting under-specified generality claims with repaired probes and training-dose/capacity axes, we give, to our knowledge, the first production-scale write-content verdict. We test 124M-7B self-trained/publicly pretrained beds, Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-FP8 (176.95B; 320,001,536 FP8 rows), and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash. Write coverage requires a sufficiently trained backbone prior, full-width readout, trainable gates; undertrained-bed intervention confirms a threshold, not a slope. At fixed budget, coverage falls from 98% (50 facts) to 12.7% (1,000); table size is not binding. Two-hop composition does not exceed the independent single-hop baseline (26% observed vs 25% expected; 15% lexical-distortion floor). Synergy remains absent across dose/load in two independent bed families. A 28-percentage-point in-context gap (given vs recalled intermediates) localizes failure to retrieval-for-reasoning, not gate access. Writes are independently retrievable, precisely addressable, reversible atoms, not composable into reasoning. A layered protocol, the first, to our knowledge, to cover compositionality in behavioral memory evaluation, separates baseline, synergy and distortion floor. Any addressed/key-value memory must report coverage, synergy ratio and distortion rate before deployment claims. Composition must be system-orchestrated; multi-constraint queries should explicitly chain written atoms. In-context controls show given intermediate entities are exploited at twice the implicit rate. Production load fits exponential interference ($R^2=0.98$); its mechanism, between budget dilution and write interference, remains open. All numbers are recomputed from archived raw logs/JSON; a fresh 52-target production rerun gives 52/52, exactly matching archived baselines.

title: Sufficient Frame Subsets for Video Understanding
abstract: Understanding when during a video a model makes its critical observations is essential for interpreting video-understanding systems. However, existing attribution methods often spread evidence diffusely across near-duplicate frames. We introduce Sufficient Frame Subsets: compact sets of frames in which all other frames are masked, yet each subset independently preserves the model's prediction. We evaluate our method on two complementary benchmarks, UCF101 and Something-Something v2, using both CNN- and transformer-based architectures. Our results show that the proposed algorithm identifies highly compact and effective frame subsets for explaining model decisions. We also find that models capable of relying on a greater number of sufficient frame subsets tend to perform better, possibly because they are more robust, consistent with prior research. Finally, the extracted frame subsets help us analyze model failure cases, reveal which aspects of a video the model has learned to emphasize, and identify opportunities for improving future training procedures.

title: From Clinical Risk Prediction to Operational Decisions: An Uncertainty-Aware Framework for ICU Staffing
abstract: Advances in electronic health records (EHR) and large-scale critical care databases have enabled the development of machine learning models for the early detection of patient deterioration. While these models often achieve strong predictive performance for outcomes such as sepsis and mortality, most studies evaluate them purely on discrimination metrics. This leaves a critical gap: how to systematically translate probabilistic clinical risk estimates into downstream operational decisions under real-world constraints, such as shift rigidity and hiring delays. This study proposes an uncertainty-aware anticipatory staffing framework that bridges short-term patient risk prediction and staff planning without altering the upstream predictive model. Instead of relying on naive deterministic aggregation or fixed safety buffers, the framework explicitly models dynamic predictive uncertainty and evaluates extreme shortage exposure using Conditional Value-at-Risk (CVaR). These aggregated, risk-calibrated demand signals are then embedded into an hourly rolling-horizon scheduling policy to generate delay-constrained staffing decisions. Evaluated on realistic trajectories from the MIMIC-IV database, the proposed framework demonstrates a favorable cost-shortage trade-off compared to deterministic and purely reactive baselines. Pareto frontier analysis illustrates how uncertainty-aware demand construction changes resource allocation under varying safety preferences, while stress testing confirms the framework's operational robustness even when subjected to systematic predictive bias in the form of calibration drift. By formalizing this translation layer, this work provides a principled, transparent pathway for safely integrating probabilistic AI outputs into high-stakes healthcare operational systems.

title: SENRI: Understanding the Space-Event Nexus in Real-Life Videos
abstract: Human memories are organized in a way that connects events with their corresponding spatial contexts. An AI assistant should also be able to memorize and recall the nexus of events and spaces. Thus we introduce SENRI, a task that studies this space--event connection in long, continuous real-life egocentric video. It contains six task types in two directions: Event$\rightarrow$Space, which recovers spatial knowledge from event cues, and Space$\rightarrow$Event, which retrieves events from regions and trajectories. To evaluate this, we build SENRI-Bench, containing 500 manually annotated multiple-choice questions over 10 uninterrupted self-recorded videos with around 25.3 hours of content. Also, we evaluate three typical long video understanding paradigms: direct perception, evidence seeking, and persistent memory. The task remains challenging across all three paradigms, highlighting substantial room for improvement. Then we show two representative failure modes of existing memory methods and address these evidence gaps with SENRI-Agent, a controller that uses Target-Guided Visual Check (TGVC) to propose local visual check tasks for parallel verifiers and integrate the reports into a working memory to help with reasoning. Built upon existing memory systems, SENRI-Agent improves the performance of existing baselines without modifying their stored memories. We hope SENRI will provide valuable insights into how real-life egocentric understanding should be evaluated, reveal the gaps in existing approaches, and offer a possible direction for improvement.

title: ROC space with four example classifiers
abstract: The ROC space, with the four example prediction results A, B, C and C′ from the Receiver operating characteristic article. The horizontal axis is the false positive rate, FPR = FP / (FP + TN), which equals 1 − specificity. The vertical axis is the true positive rate, TPR = TP / (TP + FN), which equals sensitivity.Each point comes from a contingency table of 100 positive and 100 negative instances:A: TP 63, FN 37, FP 28, TN 72, so FPR = 0.28, TPR = 0.63B: TP 77, FN 23, FP 77, TN 23, so FPR = 0.77, TPR = 0.77 (on the diagonal)C: TP 24, FN 76, FP 88, TN 12, so FPR = 0.88, TPR = 0.24 (below the diagonal)C′: C with every prediction reversed (TP 76, FN 24, FP 12, TN 88), so FPR = 0.12, TPR = 0.76The dashed diagonal is the line of random guesses. Results in the shaded half above it are better than random, and results below it are worse. Each point is labeled with its coordinates. The center point (0.5, 0.5) is marked with an open circle, and C′ is the reflection of C through that point. The point (0, 1) is perfect classification.Sources: Fawcett, T. (2006), "An introduction to ROC analysis", Pattern Recognition Letters 27(8): 861–874, doi:10.1016/j.patrec.2005.10.010 (ROC space, the diagonal, and reversing a worse-than-random classifier). title: Shared-Private Cross-Modal Discrepancy Learning for Imbalanced Multi-Source Audio-Visual Deepfake Detection
abstract: Audio-visual deepfake detectors are often trained under a single dataset or manipulation regime, but multi-source training collections may contain heterogeneous attacks and uneven source distributions. Training separate detectors for each source is inefficient, while a single shared detector may be biased toward dominant source-specific patterns. We study known-source imbalanced multi-source audio-visual deepfake detection using FakeAVCeleb and LAV-DF, where source identity is supplied during training and inference. To address this setting, we build on the Multi-Scale Cross-Modal Transformer Encoder (MSCT) and propose Pre-MSCT Shared-Private Feature Fusion. Our method routes \texttt{[CLS]}-augmented audio and visual tokens into a shared stream and source-specific private streams before the first MSCT block, while retaining its internal multi-scale self-attention (MSSA), differential cross-modal attention (DCA), and feed-forward operations. The shared stream models cross-source reusable evidence, while the private streams retain source-dependent residual variations. A domain-aware gated residual fusion module injects selected private evidence into the shared representation for the main fused prediction. Experiments under two controlled source-composition protocols show improved macro and worst-source AUC compared with the MRDF and MSCT baselines. These results support shared-private cross-modal discrepancy learning in the evaluated two-source setting with known source identity.

title: P2N: Reusing Deep Representations for Greater Effective Depth
abstract: Mathematical problem solving and autonomous agents are increasingly important applications of language models, demanding stronger reasoning capabilities. Computational depth is a key resource for such reasoning, but adding model layers increases both training and inference costs, while test-time scaling incurs substantial additional inference computation. We introduce P2N (Previous to Next), which reuses the previous token's deep representations, already available during generation, to increase effective computational depth with negligible decoding overhead. Specifically, P2N adds the previous token's deep hidden state to the current token's shallow representation, allowing subsequent layers to build on previously completed deep computation. This recurrence extends effective computational depth across tokens, while introducing only a single vector addition per decoding step. We train the recurrence using parallel Jacobi updates restricted to a middle-layer core. Experiments with Qwen-style models show that, at 1.5B parameters, P2N improves GSM8K accuracy by over 10 percentage points under both zero-shot and few-shot prompting, with nearly unchanged decoding latency. The benefits also extend to language modeling and average performance on general downstream benchmarks. on general downstream benchmarks.

title: Generative Structural Theory v1.23 — Connecting the Class C Evaluation with Closure-Preserving Sub-relations
abstract: GST v1.19 stored, for the fixed cut z_t of twelve pairs, a list of 59 sub-relations as the set C_2 of its class C evaluation; GST v1.20-v1.22 described, counted and analysed the family H_lt(z_t) of the proper sub-relations of z_t that keep its reflexive transitive closure, which also has 59 members. This manuscript connects the two by members, not by counts, and keeps three objects apart: the set E_alg that the evaluator's loop and acceptance condition define, the set E_stored of the elements of the stored list, and the set C_2 of the paper's definition. (T2a) E_alg = H_lt(z_t), by an argument based on existing computation results (the registered B1 check of v1.20) and on the drafting side's static reading of the evaluator, with no new enumeration. (T2b) E_stored = H_lt(z_t), and the stored list has no repeated element, confirmed by a pre-registered, LOCKed machine comparison (a single run, no automatic correction, no rerun; word EQUAL), which builds the reference set in two ways that must agree and checks four controls first. Hence E_stored = H_lt(z_t) = E_alg as sets, relations being identified with their integer codes. (T2c) Every member of C_2, where its definition applies, lies in H_lt(z_t), by the definition alone, without D2 or a check of condition C-cone; the converse inclusion holds if the recorded certified set V of the v1.18 runs is the V of those runs. So C_2 = H_lt(z_t) holds under that assumption; it is not established without it, and the assumption is undetermined. (T3) Through the equalities of T2a and T2b, the v1.22 results for z_t hold for E_alg and E_stored: five pairs lie in every member, there are four inclusion-minimal members, of 7, 7, 8 and 8 pairs, the least number of pairs is 7, and the stored answer y = z_t - {1>3} is one of the seven maximal members and is not inclusion-minimal. A short lemma says why removing the maximum z_t does not change the essential pairs, the inclusion-minimal members or the members of minimum cardinality. These are structural consequences; they do not explain why the procedure stored y. Nothing is claimed about the provenance of the stored file, other cuts, or the classification inside components.

title: PDF token cost per page: Claude vs Gemini, and PDF vs pasted text
abstract: Input tokens for text, table and scanned PDF pages (1 to 10 pages) on Claude Opus/Sonnet 5.5, Claude Haiku 4.5 and Gemini 3.x, compared with pasting the same content as text. Headline: one page of text costs 2,347 tokens as a PDF on Claude 5.5 but 728 when the same text is pasted (69% less). Gemini charges a flat ~560 tokens per PDF page whatever is on it. Source page, chart and method: https://tokensave.app/data/pdf-token-cost Related: image token cost by resolution (https://tokensave.app/data/image-token-cost) Measured: 2026-10-18 License: CC BY 4.0 Key findings Claude reads each PDF page as text and as an image. A text page costs 2,347 tokens on Claude 5.5; a scanned page with no text layer costs 1,600 (the image part alone). Pasting text is much cheaper on Claude: 728 tokens instead of 2,347 for the same page. Gemini charges a flat rate: text, table and scanned pages all cost 561 tokens; 10 pages cost 5,601. On Gemini a PDF can beat pasting: the table page costs 561 tokens as a PDF and 777 pasted as CSV (28% less as a PDF). Cost grows in a straight line with pages: 10 text pages cost 23,236 tokens on Claude 5.5. Files pdf-token-cost.csv: one row per input with input, label, kind, pages, tokens for claude55, claude45, gemini, gpt (pasted text only) and per-page values pdf-token-cost.json: the same data plus the pasted text used Data Input Claude Opus/Sonnet 5.5 Claude Haiku 4.5 Gemini 3.x GPT (o200k) PDF, text, 1 page 2,347 2,115 561 – PDF, text, 5 pages 11,631 10,499 2,801 – PDF, text, 10 pages 23,236 20,979 5,601 – PDF, table, 1 page 2,481 2,278 561 – PDF, scanned image, 1 page 1,600 1,592 561 – Same page pasted as text 728 503 455 461 Same table pasted as CSV text 913 720 777 629 Method A4 PDFs made with ReportLab: one page of English prose (about 420 words), the same page repeated to 5 and 10 pages, a page with a 35-row table, and a scanned version of the text page (150 dpi image, no text layer). Claude: each PDF sent through Claude Code (claude -p, stream-json input) as a document block with a one-character message; input tokens minus the same run without the PDF. Opus 5.5 and Sonnet 5.5 gave identical counts. Gemini: per-file token count shown by Google AI Studio for Gemini 3.8 Flash. Pasted text: prompt counter minus its one start token. GPT: OpenAI bills PDF input as extracted text plus page images, which could not be reproduced without the API, so GPT is given for pasted text only (tiktoken, o200k_base). Limitations One page design. Denser pages, small fonts or many images will cost more on Claude. Default settings; Gemini's media resolution option changes its per-page count. Input tokens only; price per token differs by model. Citation TokenSave (2026). title: Breaking the 1/3 Barrier for Approximate Nash Equilibria in Symmetric Bimatrix Games
abstract: We give the first unconditional family of polynomial-time algorithms that breaks the $1/3$ approximation barrier for symmetric bimatrix games. For every fixed $δ>0$, an algorithm in this family computes a symmetric $(1-1/\sqrt{2}+δ)$-approximate Nash equilibrium, improving on the previous best guarantee of $(1/3+δ)$ due to Kontogiannis and Spirakis [2011].

title: Learning When to Abort in Transformer Planning: A Mechanistic Study
abstract: Planning does not by itself imply the ability to recognise errors, but recognising errors can improve planning capacity. In this paper, we study this phenomenon in Transformer planning. To analyze the inner mechanism, we follow the approach of Wang et al. (2024) and abstract planning as path-finding in graphs. In this setting, we train the model to detect the error of invalid transitions, i.e., after the model generates a next node that is not adjacent with the current node, the model should then generate a special abort token x. For expressiveness, we construct a Transformer with feed-forward width $O(|V|)$ for any fixed graph with node set $V$. It can detect all possible invalid transitions, and select a valid next node if the prefix is valid. We then propose a worst-case lower bound on feed-forward width, which makes the detector's linear width near-optimal up to logarithmic factors. In trained models, we demonstrate that invalid-transition detection increases previous-node attention, and most of the valid--invalid separation locates in the feed-forward network's output. This accords with our theoretical insights. Finally, we use this error detection to improve the model's performance: at inference, generating the abort token x will directly cause an external procedure to discard the attempt and restart from the original prompt. Experiments show that error detection combined with retry improves model's planning reliability on graphs, Countdown, and mazes.

title: MoCKEFA: Model-Conditioned Keyframe Extraction and Fair Attribution for Video Model Explanation
abstract: We show that a video can be represented with just a few keyframes without sacrificing a given model's belief about the video. Our method is the first of its kind that extracts these keyframes conditioned on the model's prediction, which is massively helpful for building explainable video models. We then fairly distribute the importance of the video to the model among the keyframes with game theoretically fair Shapley values. Through qualitative and quantitative experiments, we show that keyframe attribution is superior to the traditional frame attribution. Further, we conduct preliminary exploration on highlighting the important changes among the frames by looking at the differences between adjacent keyframes.

title: Polynomial Density Learning of Spherical Gaussian Mixtures with a Minimum-Weight Bound
abstract: We give a polynomial-time improper density learner for mixtures of at most k identity-covariance Gaussians in ℝ^d whose nonzero mixing weights are at least a supplied w_min > 0. The means are unrestricted and need not be separated, linearly independent, or contained in a bounded ball. Training samples, real-arithmetic operations, and the cost of each output sample are polynomial in d, k, w_min⁻¹, ε⁻¹, log(1/δ), where ε is total-variation accuracy and 1−δ is training confidence. In particular, uniformly weighted mixtures admit joint-polynomial density learning without geometric assumptions. The construction extends a positive-atom moment cover to bounded-radius Gaussian location mixtures through compressed radial normalization. Fresh Gaussian split views then yield exact positive localization and globally pruned radius refinement without accumulated noise. At the terminal radius, full routed positive semidefinite moment matrices learn tensor subspaces, while an observable quadratic loss under a common mixture reference learns density coefficients from the original samples. This separation avoids a failure of per-bin Hermite density estimation: a far component of tiny routing mass can have exponentially large local Hermite coefficients. Randomized Hermite evaluation, clipping, and capped rejection sampling yield a valid nonnegative output distribution. The dependence on the minimum original weight is substantive; arbitrary-weight joint-polynomial learning remains outside the theorem.

title: FracTS: Hierarchical and Autoregressive Time Series Generation
abstract: Time series are ubiquitous across different domains, and the growing use of synthetic data for privacy-preserving sharing, data augmentation, and stress testing makes time series generation increasingly important. Early generative approaches are predominantly autoregressive, which can suffer from low sample diversity, error accumulation, and difficulty modeling long-range dependencies. In this paper, we introduce FracTS, a hierarchical, coarse-to-fine autoregressive model for multivariate time series generation. Inspired by fractal generative modeling developed for images, FracTS adapts the paradigm from 2D to 1D sequences by learning a multi-scale representation that captures global trajectory structure at coarse scales and local dynamics at fine scales while following the autoregressive nature of time series. In contrast to unstructured images, time series are structured, allowing easy automated or designated temporal feature processing optimized for the model, and global (static) feature extraction describing the instances that generate the corresponding time series in the collection. We incorporate them in the generation process to further improve the generation quality. The design naturally handles multivariate dependencies and improves long-horizon temporal coherence without requiring fixed-length inputs. Experiments on five datasets (two conditional, three unconditional) conducted against seven baselines show that FracTS consistently outperforms baselines across marginal distribution and predictive ML utility, and correlation preservation in the unconditional setting. In particular, the predictive ML utility is averagely improved by 100.0% and 75.0-81.0% for unconditional and conditional time series datasets compared to the best baseline (relative error computed on dataset-averaged raw values). Code is available at: https://github.com/BetterdataLabs/fracts.

title: Aligning Language Models with Indigenous Community Cosmovision through Constitutional AI
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are predominantly trained on corpora that reflect Western, anglophone worldviews. This asymmetry is not neutral: when a model answers questions about territory, community authority, or the relationship with nature, it does so from assumptions that may be alien to the communities using the system. This paper presents a system for aligning language models with the ethical principles of Indigenous communities in Latin America. Drawing on interviews with five Indigenous leaders and defenders, we built an operational cultural constitution grounded in an Indigenous cosmovision, with 12 principles. On this basis, we implemented a Constitutional AI (CAI) pipeline in two phases: supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and direct preference optimization (DPO). The base models were Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct. With only 24 preference pairs, improvements were modest but detectable in intergenerational transmission, linguistic caution, and consultation and consent. Qualitative analysis reveals that the SFT phase was responsible for the primary shift in alignment, while DPO refined specific categories. The system was deployed in a conversational interface with retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) that allows communities to feed the knowledge base, turning alignment into a participatory cycle. We argue the architecture is functional and will scale qualitatively once the corpus is expanded and computing constraints are resolved. The work constitutes a first iteration of an epistemic justice mechanism for value alignment in the Global South.
